# Section A — Reading for all and there exists

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise M, Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Which of the following are true and which are false?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**i.** **for every** real $x$, $x^2$ is rational

&nbsp;&nbsp;**ii.** **there exists** a real $x$ such that $x^2$ is rational

&nbsp;&nbsp;**iii.** **for every** real $x$, $x^2>x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**iv.** **there exists** a real $x$ such that $x^2>x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**v.** **for every** real $x$, $x^3>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**vi.** **there exists** a real $x$ such that $x^3>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**vii.** **for every** real $x$ and $y$, $x^2+y^2>2xy$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**viii.** **there exists** real $x$ and $y$ such that $x^2+y^2>2xy$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**i, iii, v and vii are false. ii, iv, vi and viii are true.**

A "for every" statement falls to one counterexample. A "there exists" statement is proved by one witness.

| | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **i** | False | $x=\sqrt[4]{2}$ gives $x^2=\sqrt2$, which is irrational |
| **ii** | True | $x=1$ gives $x^2=1$ |
| **iii** | False | $x=\tfrac12$ gives $x^2=\tfrac14$, which is not greater than $\tfrac12$ |
| **iv** | True | $x=2$ gives $4>2$ |
| **v** | False | $x=-1$ gives $x^3=-1$ |
| **vi** | True | $x=1$ gives $1>0$ |
| **vii** | False | $x=y=1$ gives $2>2$, which fails |
| **viii** | True | $x=1,\ y=0$ gives $1>0$ |

**Look at vii carefully.** Rearranging, $x^2+y^2-2xy=(x-y)^2$, which is **at least** $0$ and equals $0$ exactly
when $x=y$. So the statement fails only on the line $x=y$, but one failure is all a "for every" can stand.

**The pattern in the pairs.** Each even-numbered statement is the "there exists" version of the one before it. A
false "for every" can sit next to a true "there exists" with the same inside, as here in all four pairs.
:::

## Question 2 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise N, Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Which of the following are true and which are false?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**i.** **for all** real $x$ **there exists** a real $y$ such that: $x>y$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**ii.** **for all** real $x$ **there exists** a real $y$ such that: $y>x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**iii.** **for all** real $y$ **there exists** a real $x$ such that: $x>y$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**iv.** **for all** real $y$ **there exists** a real $x$ such that: $y>x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**v.** **there exists** a real $x$ such that **for all** real $y$: $x>y$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**vi.** **there exists** a real $x$ such that **for all** real $y$: $y>x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**vii.** **there exists** a real $y$ such that **for all** real $x$: $x>y$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**viii.** **there exists** a real $y$ such that **for all** real $x$: $y>x$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**i, ii, iii and iv are true. v, vi, vii and viii are false.**

**The first four.** The "for all" comes first, so the first letter is given to you and you choose the second
letter afterwards, knowing the first.

- **i.** Given $x$, take $y=x-1$. Then $x>y$.
- **ii.** Given $x$, take $y=x+1$. Then $y>x$.
- **iii.** Given $y$, take $x=y+1$. Then $x>y$.
- **iv.** Given $y$, take $x=y-1$. Then $y>x$.

**The last four.** The "there exists" comes first, so **one** number must be fixed before the second letter is
seen, and it must then work against every value of that letter.

- **v.** This claims a largest real number. Whatever $x$ you fix, $y=x+1$ gives $x>y$ false.
- **vi.** This claims a smallest real number. Whatever $x$ you fix, $y=x-1$ gives $y>x$ false.
- **vii.** The same claim as vi with the letters renamed. Take $x=y-1$.
- **viii.** The same claim as v with the letters renamed. Take $x=y+1$.

**The inequality never changes in spirit. Only the order does**, and the order alone decides the truth value.
:::

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement about the positive integer $n$:

> Statement $(*)$: *The sum of the four consecutive integers, the smallest of which is $n$, is a multiple of $6$.*

Which **one** of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Statement $(*)$ is true for all values of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Statement $(*)$ is true for all values of $n$ which are odd, but not for any other values of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** Statement $(*)$ is true for all values of $n$ which are multiples of $3$, but not for any other values of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Statement $(*)$ is true for all values of $n$ which are multiples of $6$, but not for any other values of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** Statement $(*)$ is not true for any value of $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

**Step 1 — find the sum.**

$$n+(n+1)+(n+2)+(n+3)=4n+6 .$$

**Step 2 — decide when it is a multiple of $6$.** Since $4n+6=6+4n$, and $6$ is already a multiple of $6$, the sum
is a multiple of $6$ exactly when $4n$ is. Now $4n=2\times2n$ and $6=2\times3$, so we can cancel the common
factor $2$: this happens exactly when $3$ divides $2n$. As $3$ is prime and does not divide $2$, that means
$3$ divides $n$.

$$4n+6 \text{ is a multiple of } 6 \iff n \text{ is a multiple of } 3 .$$

**Step 3 — read the options as quantified statements.** Each of B, C and D makes **two** claims: "true for all
values of this kind" **and** "not true for any other value".

- **A** fails at $n=1$: the sum is $10$.
- **B** fails at $n=1$: this is odd, and the sum is $10$.
- **C** is exactly the result of Step 2.
- **D** has the first half right, because multiples of $6$ do work. But "not for any other value" fails at $n=3$,
  where $3+4+5+6=18$.
- **E** fails at $n=3$ too, because one working value is all it takes to break "not for any value".
:::

## Question 4 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement:

$(*)$ **For all** real numbers $x$, **if** $x<k$ **then** $x^2<k$

What is the complete set of values of $k$ for which $(*)$ is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** no real numbers

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $k>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $k<1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $k\le1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $0<k<1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $0<k\le1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** all real numbers
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A — no real numbers.**

**Step 1 — write what would break $(*)$.** Negating the "for all" and the "if … then":

$$\text{there exists a real } x \text{ such that } x<k \ \text{ and }\ x^2\ge k .$$

So $(*)$ is false for a given $k$ as soon as we find **one** such $x$.

**Step 2 — find that $x$ for every $k$.** The domain is **all** real numbers, so negative values are allowed. Take
any $k$ and let

$$x=-\lvert k\rvert-2 .$$

- $x<k$, because $x$ is below $-\lvert k\rvert$, and $-\lvert k\rvert\le k$.
- $x^2=(\lvert k\rvert+2)^2\ge\lvert k\rvert+2>k$, because a number that is at least $2$ is no bigger than its
  square.

So the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails. Every value of $k$ has a counterexample, and $(*)$ is never true.

**Why E and F tempt.** If $0<x<k\le1$, then $x^2<x<k$, so the statement does hold for **positive** $x$. Those
options come from forgetting that "for all real numbers $x$" includes the negatives. For $k=\tfrac12$, the value
$x=-1$ satisfies $x<k$, yet $x^2=1$ is not below $\tfrac12$.
:::

## Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the curve

$$y=\log_{x-1}4\qquad\text{for } x>1,\ x\ne2 .$$

Which of the following statements about this curve are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $y>0$ **for every** $x$ in the domain.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $y$ is a strictly decreasing function of $x$ on the domain.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **For every** real number $y$, **there exists** a value of $x$ in the domain such that $y=\log_{x-1}4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; $y=0$ is an asymptote.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** III and IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** None of the statements is true.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**J** All four statements are true.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D — IV only.**

**Step 1 — make the curve readable.** $y=\log_{x-1}4$ means $(x-1)^y=4$. Taking natural logarithms,

$$y\ln(x-1)=\ln4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=\frac{\ln4}{\ln(x-1)} ,$$

where dividing is allowed because $x\ne2$ makes $\ln(x-1)\ne0$.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0,3.6))
for lo,hi in [(1.02,1.93),(2.07,40)]:
    x=np.linspace(lo,hi,800); ax.plot(x,np.log(4)/np.log(x-1),color='#1f77b4',lw=2)
ax.axvline(2,color='0.5',ls=':',lw=1.2); ax.axhline(0,color='#d62728',ls='--',lw=1.2,label='$y=0$: approached, never reached')
ax.plot([1.5,3],[-2,2],'o',color='#d62728')
ax.annotate('$(3/2,\\,-2)$',(1.5,-2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(12,-6),fontsize=9)
ax.annotate('$(3,\\,2)$',(3,2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(10,6),fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(1,16); ax.set_ylim(-8,8); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**I is false.** A "for every" needs one failure. At $x=\tfrac32$, $\;\ln\tfrac12<0$, so $y<0$. In fact $y=-2$.

**II is false.** Compare $x=\tfrac32$, where $y=-2$, with $x=3$, where $y=2$. As $x$ went up, $y$ went up. The
function decreases on $(1,2)$ and on $(2,\infty)$ separately, but not on the whole domain, because of the jump at
the vertical asymptote $x=2$.

**III is false.** It is a "for every $y$, there exists $x$", so its negation is "there exists a $y$ such that **no**
$x$ works". That $y$ is $0$: the numerator $\ln4$ is non-zero, so the fraction is never $0$. Equivalently,
$(x-1)^0=1\ne4$.

**IV is true.** As $x\to\infty$, $\ln(x-1)\to\infty$, so $y\to0$.

**Link between III and IV.** The value $y=0$ that breaks III is exactly the asymptote in IV: the curve gets
arbitrarily close to it and never reaches it.
:::

# Section B — Negating a definition

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
Let $S$ be a set of positive integers, for example $S$ could consist of $3$, $4$, and $8$.

A positive integer $n$ is called an $S$-number **if and only if** for every factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, the number
$m$ is a multiple of some number in $S$.

So in the above example, $9$ is an $S$-number; this is because the factors of $9$ greater than $1$ are $3$ and $9$, and
each of these is a multiple of $3$.

Positive integer $n$ is therefore **not** an $S$-number **if and only if**

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** for **every** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, there is a number in $S$ which is not a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** for **every** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, there is no number in $S$ which is a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** for **every** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, every number in $S$ is a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** for **some** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, there is a number in $S$ which is not a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** for **some** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, there is no number in $S$ which is a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** for **some** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, every number in $S$ is a factor of $m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E.**

**Step 1 — write the definition as a chain.** "$m$ is a multiple of some number in $S$" says the same as "some
number in $S$ is a factor of $m$". So

$$n \text{ is an } S\text{-number}\iff \forall m\ (\text{factor of } n,\ m>1),\ \ \exists s\in S,\ \ s \text{ is a factor of } m .$$

**Step 2 — negate, keeping the domain of $m$.**

- $\forall m$ becomes $\exists m$: "for **some** factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$".
- $\exists s$ becomes $\forall s$, and "is a factor" becomes "is not a factor": "**every** $s$ in $S$ fails to be a
  factor of $m$", which is "there is **no** number in $S$ which is a factor of $m$".

That is **E**.

**Step 3 — why the others fail.**

- **A, B, C** begin with "every", so the outer quantifier was never flipped.
- **D** says **one** number of $S$ is not a factor of $m$. The negation needs **all** of them to fail. This is the
  "there is one that fails" slip, in place of "none works".
- **F** flips both quantifiers but never negates the inside: it still says "is a factor".

**A sanity check on the example.** With $S=\{3,4,8\}$, the integer $n=2$ is not an $S$-number: its factor $m=2$ has
no factor in $S$. This matches E, and D alone could not detect it, since D would also hold for the $S$-number $9$
(take $m=3$, and $4$ is not a factor of $3$).
:::

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock B · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
A set $X$ of positive integers, with $\lvert X\rvert\ge3$, is called **cross-linked** if and only if for every number $x$ in
$X$ there exist two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $X$, both different from $x$, and a prime $p$, such that $p$ divides
each of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

Let $Y$ be a set of positive integers with $\lvert Y\rvert\ge3$.

Which of the following statements is equivalent to $Y$ being **not** cross-linked?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** For every number $x$ in $Y$, and for every two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$ with $y\ne x$ and $z\ne x$, there is no prime which divides all of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** For every number $x$ in $Y$ there exist two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$, both different from $x$, such that no prime divides all of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** There exists a number $x$ in $Y$, and there exist two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$ with $y\ne x$ and $z\ne x$, such that no prime divides all of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** There exists a number $x$ in $Y$ such that for every two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$ with $y\ne x$ and $z\ne x$, there is no prime which divides all of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** There exists a number $x$ in $Y$ such that for every two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$ with $y\ne x$ and $z\ne x$, there is a prime which divides $x$ but divides neither $y$ nor $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** For every number $x$ in $Y$ there exist two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$, both different from $x$, and a prime $p$, such that $p$ divides $x$ but $p$ does not divide $y$ and $p$ does not divide $z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.**

**Step 1 — the chain.**

$$\text{cross-linked}\iff\forall x\ \ \exists(y,z)\ \ \exists p:\ \ p \text{ divides each of } x,y,z .$$

**Step 2 — negate in two passes.** Flip every quantifier in order, then negate the inside.

$$\text{not cross-linked}\iff\exists x\ \ \forall(y,z)\ \ \forall p:\ \ p \text{ does not divide all of } x,y,z .$$

**Step 3 — translate back.** "For every prime $p$, $p$ does not divide all three" is the same as "**no** prime
divides all three". So: there exists $x$ such that for every pair $y,z$, no prime divides all of $x,y,z$. That is
**D**.

**Step 4 — the wrong options.**

| Option | Chain | What went wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $\forall x\ \forall(y,z)$ | the outer quantifier was not flipped, so this is far too strong |
| **B** | $\forall x\ \exists(y,z)$ | neither of the first two was flipped |
| **C** | $\exists x\ \exists(y,z)$ | the second was not flipped: one bad pair does not stop another pair working |
| **E** | $\exists x\ \forall(y,z)\ \exists p$ | the prime quantifier was not flipped, and the inside was rewritten |
| **F** | $\forall x\ \exists(y,z)\ \exists p$ | nothing was flipped, and the inside was rewritten |

**The C trap in one example.** Take $Y=\{2,3,4,6,9,12\}$. This set **is** cross-linked: $2,4,6,12$ share the prime
$2$, and $3,6,9,12$ share the prime $3$, so every number has two partners. Yet C's condition holds, with $x=2$ and the
pair $3,4$. One failing pair proves nothing, because the definition only asked for **one** good pair.
:::

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
A student makes the following claim:

> If $f$ is a real-valued function such that, for some constant $a$, $\;\dfrac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}=a\;$ for all real values of $x$, then there exists a constant $k$ such that $f(x)=kx+a$ for all real values of $x$.

Examine their claim above, and determine which of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The claim is true.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $f(x)=2x+1$ is a counterexample to the claim.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $f(x)=\sin x$ is a counterexample to the claim.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(x)=\tan x$ is a counterexample to the claim.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $f(x)=\cos x$ is a counterexample to the claim.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $f(x)=-x$ is a counterexample to the claim.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

**Step 1 — what a counterexample must do.** The claim has the shape "if $H$ then $C$", with quantifiers inside both
halves:

- $H$: **there exists** $a$ such that, **for all** $x$, $\dfrac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}=a$.
- $C$: **there exists** $k$ such that, **for all** $x$, $f(x)=kx+a$.

A counterexample makes $H$ **true** and $C$ **false**. Note that making $C$ false needs **every** $k$ to fail.

**Step 2 — test each option.**

| Option | $\dfrac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}$ | $H$ true? | $C$ false? | Counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **B** $\;2x+1$ | $1$ | yes, $a=1$ | no: $k=2$ works | no |
| **C** $\;\sin x$ | $0$ | yes, $a=0$ | **yes**: $\sin x$ is not a straight line | **yes** |
| **D** $\;\tan x$ | not defined at $x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ | no: $\tan x$ is not defined for all real $x$ | — | no |
| **E** $\;\cos x$ | $\cos x$ | no: not constant | — | no |
| **F** $\;-x$ | $0$ | yes, $a=0$ | no: $k=-1$ works | no |

**Step 3 — check C properly.** If $\sin x=kx$ for all $x$, then $x=\pi$ gives $0=k\pi$, so $k=0$. But then $\sin x=0$
for all $x$, which is false at $x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. So no $k$ works, and since C is a counterexample, the claim is false and A goes too.

**D is the subtle one.** It looks right, because $\tan$ is odd. But the claim is about functions with the average
equal to $a$ **for all real values of $x$**, and $\tan x$ has no value at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. An object outside the
domain of a statement cannot be a counterexample to it.
:::

# Section C — What "for every" forces

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
The region $R$ in the $(x,y)$-plane consists of all points satisfying both

$$\lvert y-x^2\rvert<2\qquad\text{and}\qquad x+y<4 .$$

Which of the following claims about points in $R$ are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I:** **For every** $(x,y)\in R$, $\;y\le6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II:** **For every** $(x,y)\in R$, $\;y>-2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III:** **For every** $(x,y)\in R$, $\;x\le2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** None of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**G — II and III only.**

**Step 1 — rewrite the conditions.** $\lvert y-x^2\rvert<2$ means $x^2-2<y<x^2+2$, and $x+y<4$ means $y<4-x$. So

$$x^2-2<y<x^2+2\qquad\text{and}\qquad y<4-x .$$

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0,4.4))
x=np.linspace(-3.6,2.6,800)
ax.plot(x,x**2-2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='$y=x^2-2$'); ax.plot(x,x**2+2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,ls='--',label='$y=x^2+2$')
ax.plot(x,4-x,color='#2ca02c',lw=2,label='$y=4-x$')
ax.fill_between(x,x**2-2,np.minimum(x**2+2,4-x),where=(x>-3)&(x<2),color='#7a5195',alpha=0.22,label='$R$')
ax.axhline(6,color='0.5',ls=':',lw=1.2); ax.plot([-2.9],[6.5],'o',color='#d62728',ms=7)
ax.annotate('$(-2.9,\\,6.5)\\in R$\nabove $y=6$: kills I',(-2.9,6.5),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(34,6),fontsize=9,color='#d62728',arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->',color='#d62728',lw=1.1))
ax.set_ylim(-3,9); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9,loc='lower left')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Step 2 — find the range of $x$.** A point of $R$ needs $x^2-2<y<4-x$, so $x^2-2<4-x$:

$$x^2+x-6<0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x+3)(x-2)<0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad-3<x<2 .$$

**III is true,** since every point of $R$ has $x<2$.

**II is true.** Every point has $y>x^2-2$, and $x^2-2\ge-2$ because $x^2\ge0$. So $y>-2$.

**I is false.** A "for every" falls to one point. The region's top left corner approaches $(-3,7)$, so look near
there. Take $(-2.9,\ 6.5)$:

- $x^2=8.41$, so $\lvert y-x^2\rvert=1.91<2$ ✓
- $x+y=3.6<4$ ✓

This point is in $R$ and has $y=6.5>6$.

**The trap in I.** Testing points near the origin suggests that $y$ stays small. The extreme is at the far corner, so
always ask where the region reaches furthest in the direction the claim is about.
:::

---

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following inequality:

$$(*):\quad a\lvert x\rvert+1\le\lvert x-2\rvert$$

where $a$ is a real constant.

Which one of the following describes the complete set of values of $a$ such that $(*)$ is **true for all real $x$**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $a\le\tfrac32$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $a\le1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $a\le\tfrac12$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $a\le0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $a\le-\tfrac12$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $a\le-1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $a\le-\tfrac32$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** There are no such values of $a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E — $a\le-\tfrac12$.**

**Step 1 — use the "for all" at the most useful $x$.** The right-hand side is smallest at $x=2$, where it is $0$. Since
$(*)$ must hold there too,

$$2a+1\le0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\le-\tfrac12 .$$

So no larger $a$ can work. This rules out A, B, C and D, and it leaves open whether all such $a$ do work.

**Step 2 — check that every $a\le-\tfrac12$ works.** Since $\lvert x\rvert\ge0$, lowering $a$ lowers the left-hand side. So
it is enough to check $a=-\tfrac12$, which is to show

$$1\le\lvert x-2\rvert+\tfrac12\lvert x\rvert\quad\text{for all real } x .$$

Let $h(x)=\lvert x-2\rvert+\tfrac12\lvert x\rvert$. On each interval it is a straight line:

| Interval | $h(x)$ | Gradient |
|---|---|---|
| $x<0$ | $2-\tfrac32x$ | $-\tfrac32$ |
| $0\le x<2$ | $2-\tfrac12x$ | $-\tfrac12$ |
| $x\ge2$ | $\tfrac32x-2$ | $+\tfrac32$ |

So $h$ falls until $x=2$ and then rises. Its minimum is $h(2)=1$, and the inequality holds for every $x$.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-5,7,800); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0,3.8))
ax.plot(x,np.abs(x-2),color='#1f77b4',lw=2.2,label='$y=|x-2|$')
ax.plot(x,-0.5*np.abs(x)+1,color='#2ca02c',lw=2,label='$a=-1/2$: touches at $x=2$, never above')
ax.plot(x,-0.3*np.abs(x)+1,color='#d62728',lw=1.6,ls='--',label='$a=-0.3$: above at $x=2$, so fails')
ax.plot([2],[0],'o',color='k',ms=5); ax.axhline(0,color='0.7',lw=.8); ax.axvline(0,color='0.7',lw=.8)
ax.set_ylim(-3,6); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**The two jobs.** One $x$ was enough to **rule out** values of $a$. Keeping the remaining values needed an argument
over **every** $x$. That is the difference between disproving a "for all" and proving one.
:::

---

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q19</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the quadratic graphs given by $\;f(x)=ax^2+bx+c\;$ and $\;g(x)=px^2+qx+r$

If $f'(x)>g'(x)$ **for all real $x$**, which of the following is/are **necessarily** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $a>p$ and $b>q$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $a=p$ and $b>q$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $b>q$ and $c>r$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C — II only.**

**Step 1 — write the condition.** Differentiating,

$$f'(x)-g'(x)=2(a-p)x+(b-q)>0\quad\text{for all real } x .$$

**Step 2 — use "for all".** The left-hand side is a straight line in $x$. If $a\ne p$, its gradient is non-zero, so it takes
every real value, negative ones included, and the condition fails. Therefore

$$a=p .$$

The line is then the constant $b-q$, and the condition becomes $b-q>0$, so $b>q$.

**Step 3 — the three statements.**

- **II is true.** It is exactly what Step 2 proved.
- **I is false.** It requires $a>p$, and Step 2 showed $a=p$.
- **III is false.** $c$ and $r$ vanish on differentiating, so the condition says nothing about them. For example, $f=x^2+2x$ and $g=x^2+x+5$ have $f'-g'=1>0$ for all $x$, yet $c=0<5=r$.

**The instinct to resist.** "$f'$ is bigger" sounds like it should make the leading coefficient bigger. But a bigger
leading coefficient only makes $f'$ bigger on one side, and "for all real $x$" covers both sides.
:::

---

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q13</span>

::: {.question}
$\mathrm{f}(x)$ is a function for which

$$\int_0^3\big(\mathrm{f}(x)\big)^2\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_0^3\mathrm{f}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_0^1\mathrm{f}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Which of the following claims about $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is/are **necessarily** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}(x)\le0$ **for some** $x$ with $1\le x\le3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $\displaystyle\int_0^3\mathrm{f}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\le\int_0^1\mathrm{f}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** neither of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** I and II
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D — I and II.**

**II first.** Rearranging the given equation,

$$\int_0^3\mathrm{f}\,\mathrm{d}x-\int_0^1\mathrm{f}\,\mathrm{d}x=-\int_0^3\mathrm{f}^2\,\mathrm{d}x .$$

Since $\mathrm{f}^2\ge0$ everywhere, $\int_0^3\mathrm{f}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\ge0$, so the right-hand side is at most $0$. That is II.

**I by negating it.** Statement I is a "for some". To test it, write its negation:

$$\text{for all } x \text{ with } 1\le x\le3,\quad\mathrm{f}(x)>0 .$$

Suppose this negation were true. Split the integral on the left of the rearranged equation:

$$\int_0^3\mathrm{f}\,\mathrm{d}x-\int_0^1\mathrm{f}\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_1^3\mathrm{f}\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

which gives

$$\int_0^3\mathrm{f}^2\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_1^3\mathrm{f}\,\mathrm{d}x=0 .$$

The first integral is at least $0$, and the second would be **strictly positive**, because $\mathrm{f}>0$ on all of
$[1,3]$. Their sum could not be $0$. So the negation is false, and I is true.

**The move to remember.** A "for some" that is hard to prove directly can be attacked by assuming its negation, a
"for all", which gives you something strong to work with.
:::

---

## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
A selection, $S$, of $n$ terms is taken from the arithmetic sequence $1,4,7,10,\dots,70$.

Consider the following statement:

$(*)$ There are two distinct terms in $S$ whose sum is $74$.

What is the smallest value of $n$ for which $(*)$ is **necessarily** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $12$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $13$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $14$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $21$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $22$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $23$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C — $14$.**

**Step 1 — find the quantifiers.** "Necessarily true" means: **for every** selection of $n$ terms, **there exist** two
distinct terms summing to $74$. Its negation is: **there exists** a selection of $n$ terms with **no** such pair. So we
want the largest selection with no pair, and then one more term.

**Step 2 — group the terms.** The sequence has $\dfrac{70-1}{3}+1=24$ terms. Pair each term $t$ with $74-t$:

$$(4,70),\ (7,67),\ (10,64),\ \dots,\ (34,40) .$$

That gives $11$ pairs, using $22$ terms. Two terms are left over, and neither can be in a pair:

- $1$, because its partner would be $73$, which is not in the sequence;
- $37$, because its partner would be $37$ itself, and the terms must be distinct.

**Step 3 — build the largest selection with no pair.** Take both leftovers and **one** term from each of the $11$ pairs:

$$1,\ 37,\ 4,\ 7,\ 10,\ \dots,\ 34 .$$

That is $13$ terms with no pair summing to $74$. So $(*)$ is **not** forced when $n=13$.

**Step 4 — show $n=14$ forces a pair.** Any $14$ terms contain at most $2$ leftovers, so at least $12$ terms come from
the $11$ pairs. Two of them must then lie in the same pair, and those two sum to $74$.

**The two jobs again.** One example was enough to show that $n=13$ fails. The proof for $n=14$ had to cover **every**
selection, which is why it is a counting argument rather than an example.
:::

---

# Section D — "For some" and "possible"

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
A student draws a triangle that is acute-angled or obtuse-angled but not right-angled.

The student counts the number of straight lines that divide the triangle into two triangles, at least one of which is
right-angled.

Which of the following statements is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; The student can draw a triangle for which there is exactly $1$ such straight line.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The student can draw a triangle for which there are exactly $2$ such straight lines.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The student can draw a triangle for which there are exactly $3$ such straight lines.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D — III only.**

**Step 1 — read "can draw" as "there exists".** Each statement says **there exists** a triangle with that count. To
reject I and II we must show that **no** triangle has that count, which means counting for **every** triangle.

**Step 2 — which lines count?** A line that divides a triangle into two **triangles** must pass through a vertex and cross
the opposite side. (Any other line leaves a triangle and a quadrilateral.) Say it goes from vertex $A$ to a point $D$
on $BC$. The original has no right angle, so a right angle in a piece can only occur:

- at $D$, which makes the line the **altitude** from $A$, with its foot inside $BC$; or
- at $A$, which needs a part of angle $A$ to be $90°$, so angle $A$ must be **obtuse**.

**Step 3 — acute triangles.** All three altitudes land inside the opposite sides, and no angle is obtuse. That gives
**exactly $3$** lines.

**Step 4 — obtuse triangles.** Let the obtuse angle be at $A$.

- The altitude from $A$ lands inside $BC$: **one** line.
- The altitudes from $B$ and $C$ land outside the triangle: no lines.
- At $A$, there are **two** ways to cut off a right angle, with $\angle BAD=90°$ or with $\angle CAD=90°$. Neither is
  the altitude, since a triangle cannot have two right angles.

That is also **exactly $3$** lines.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
def tri(ax,P,col='k'):
    P=np.array(P+[P[0]]); ax.plot(P[:,0],P[:,1],color=col,lw=2)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0,3.2))
A,B,C=np.array([1.6,3.0]),np.array([0.0,0.0]),np.array([4.0,0.0])
tri(ax,[A,B,C])
def foot(P,Q,R):
    d=R-Q; return Q+d*np.dot(P-Q,d)/np.dot(d,d)
for P,Q,R in [(A,B,C),(B,A,C),(C,A,B)]:
    F=foot(P,Q,R); ax.plot([P[0],F[0]],[P[1],F[1]],color='#d62728',lw=1.6)
ax.set_title('Acute: the three altitudes',fontsize=10); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0,2.6))
A,B,C=np.array([1.4,1.2]),np.array([0.0,0.0]),np.array([5.0,0.0])
P=np.array([A,B,C,A]); ax.plot(P[:,0],P[:,1],color='k',lw=2)
ax.plot([A[0],A[0]],[A[1],0],color='#d62728',lw=1.6,label='altitude from the obtuse vertex')
# right angle at A with side AB, and with side AC
D1=np.array([A[0]+A[1]*(B[1]-A[1])/(B[0]-A[0]),0.0])
D2=np.array([A[0]+A[1]*(C[1]-A[1])/(C[0]-A[0]),0.0])
ax.plot([A[0],D1[0]],[A[1],0],color='#1f77b4',lw=1.6,label='right angle cut off at the obtuse vertex')
ax.plot([A[0],D2[0]],[A[1],0],color='#1f77b4',lw=1.6)
ax.set_title('Obtuse: one altitude and two cut-off right angles',fontsize=10); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=8,loc='lower center',bbox_to_anchor=(0.5,-0.32)); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Step 5 — conclude.** Every triangle gives exactly $3$. So III is true, and no triangle gives $1$ or $2$, so I and II are
false.
:::

---

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock D · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
Let $a$ be a real number with $a>1$, and let $f$ be a function such that

$$f(0)=1,\qquad f(2)>a^2,\qquad f(-1)<a^{-1}.$$

Consider the following four statements.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I.** $f(x)=b^x$ **for some** real number $b$ with $b>a$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II.** $f(x)=b^x$ **for some** real number $b$ with $0<b<a$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III.** $f(x)=a^{kx}$ **for some** real number $k$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV.** $f(x)=b^{x^2}$ **for some** positive real number $b$.

Which of the statements **might** be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Statement I only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Statement III only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** Statements I and III only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Statements I, II and III only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** Statements I, III and IV only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** Statements II and IV only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** Statements II, III and IV only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** All four statements.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C — I and III only.**

**"Might be true" is a "there exists".** A statement might be true when **there exists** a function of that form
meeting all three conditions. So a statement is kept by one witness, and it is rejected only by showing that **no** value of
the constant works.

**I might be true.** Take any $b>a$. Then $f(0)=1$ ✓, $f(2)=b^2>a^2$ ✓, and $f(-1)=\dfrac1b<\dfrac1a$ ✓. All three hold.

**II cannot be true.** With $0<b<a$, we get $f(2)=b^2<a^2$, which contradicts $f(2)>a^2$. This covers **every** such $b$.

**III might be true.** Take $k=2$, so $f(x)=a^{2x}=(a^2)^x$. This is form I with $b=a^2$, and $a^2>a$ because $a>1$. So
all three conditions hold.

**IV cannot be true.** Here $f(2)=b^4$ and $f(-1)=b^{(-1)^2}=b$. The conditions would need

- $b^4>a^2>1$, which forces $b>1$;
- $b<a^{-1}<1$, which forces $b<1$.

These contradict each other, so no $b$ works. $f(0)=b^0=1$ holds, but that does not rescue it.

**The trap in IV.** The square in the exponent means $f(-1)$ uses $(-1)^2=1$, so $f(-1)=b$ rather than $\tfrac1b$. Missing that
makes IV look just like I.
:::

---

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
A student chooses two distinct real numbers $x$ and $y$ with $0<x<y<1$.

The student then attempts to draw a triangle $ABC$ with:

$$AB=1,\qquad\sin A=x,\qquad\sin B=y$$

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; **For some** choice of $x$ and $y$, there is exactly **one** triangle the student could draw.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; **For some** choice of $x$ and $y$, there are exactly **two** different triangles the student could draw.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **For some** choice of $x$ and $y$, there are exactly **three** different triangles the student could draw.

(Note that congruent triangles are considered to be the same.)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C — II only.**

**Step 1 — list the angle options.** Let $\theta$ and $\phi$ be the **acute** angles with $\sin\theta=x$ and $\sin\phi=y$. As
$x<y$, we have $\theta<\phi$. Each of $A$ and $B$ can be acute or obtuse, since $\sin(180°-\alpha)=\sin\alpha$:

$$A=\theta\ \text{ or }\ 180°-\theta,\qquad B=\phi\ \text{ or }\ 180°-\phi .$$

Two angles and the side $AB$ between them fix a triangle uniquely, **provided** $A+B<180°$. So there are four cases to test.

**Step 2 — test the cases.**

| $A$ | $B$ | $A+B$ | Triangle? |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\theta$ | $\phi$ | $\theta+\phi<180°$ | **yes** |
| $180°-\theta$ | $\phi$ | $180°+(\phi-\theta)>180°$ | no |
| $\theta$ | $180°-\phi$ | $180°-(\phi-\theta)<180°$ | **yes** |
| $180°-\theta$ | $180°-\phi$ | $360°-\theta-\phi>180°$ | no |

The two surviving triangles have different angles at $B$, so they are not congruent.

**Step 3 — read the statements.** The table used nothing about $x$ and $y$ except $0<x<y<1$, so **for every** choice there
are **exactly two** triangles.

- **II** is a "for some", and one choice is enough, so it is true.
- **I** and **III** are also "for some", but the count is always $2$. **No** choice gives $1$ or $3$, so they are false.

**Why the "for some" matters.** The count turned out never to depend on the choice, and that is the surprise here. A
"for some" statement is rejected only by an argument covering every choice, and the table is that argument.
:::

---

## Question 17 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2016 · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
Consider these simultaneous equations, where $c$ is a constant:

$$y=3\sin x+2$$

$$y=x+c$$

Which of the following statements is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1** &nbsp; **For some** value of $c$: there is exactly one solution with $0\le x\le\pi$ **and** there is at least one solution with $-\pi<x<0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**2** &nbsp; **For some** value of $c$: there is exactly one solution with $0\le x\le\pi$ **and** there are no solutions with $-\pi<x<0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** &nbsp; **For some** value of $c$: there is exactly one solution with $0\le x\le\pi$ **and** there are no solutions with $x>\pi$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** 1 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** 1 and 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** 1 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** 1, 2 and 3
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**H — all three.**

**Each statement is a "for some $c$", so each one needs just one witness.** Sliding $c$ moves the line $y=x+c$ up and
down across the fixed wave, which runs between $-1$ and $5$.

**Statement 1: take $c=1$.**

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
xs=np.linspace(-np.pi,2.2*np.pi,900); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2,3.4))
ax.plot(xs,3*np.sin(xs)+2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='$y=3\\sin x+2$'); ax.plot(xs,xs+1,color='#d62728',lw=1.8,label='$y=x+1$')
for r in [-1.868,-0.538,2.585]: ax.plot(r,r+1,'o',color='#7a5195',ms=6)
ax.axvline(0,color='0.8',lw=.8); ax.axvline(np.pi,color='0.8',lw=.8); ax.axhline(0,color='0.8',lw=.8); ax.set_ylim(-3,8); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$')
ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9,loc='upper left'); ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

On $0\le x\le\pi$, the wave starts above the line ($2>1$) and ends below it ($2<\pi+1$), so they cross; and the
curve is concave there, so they cross only once, near $x\approx2.59$. On $-\pi<x<0$ they cross near $x\approx-1.87$ and $x\approx-0.54$.
So statement 1 holds.

**Statements 2 and 3: take $c=2-\pi$.** This value makes the line pass through $(\pi,2)$, which is on the wave.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
xs=np.linspace(-np.pi,2.5*np.pi,900); c=2-np.pi; fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2,3.4))
ax.plot(xs,3*np.sin(xs)+2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='$y=3\\sin x+2$'); ax.plot(xs,xs+c,color='#d62728',lw=1.8,label='$y=x+2-\\pi$')
ax.plot(np.pi,2,'o',color='#7a5195',ms=6); ax.axvline(0,color='0.8',lw=.8); ax.axvline(np.pi,color='0.8',lw=.8); ax.axhline(0,color='0.8',lw=.8)
ax.set_ylim(-5,7); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9,loc='upper left')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

- **On $0\le x<\pi$** the line is below $2$ and the wave is at least $2$, so they do not meet. With $x=\pi$, that is exactly one solution.
- **On $-\pi<x<0$** the line is below $2-\pi\approx-1.14$, while the wave is never below $-1$. No solutions, so statement 2 holds.
- **On $\pi<x<2\pi$** the wave is below $2$ and the line is above $2$. No solutions.
- **For $x\ge2\pi$** the line is at least $2+\pi>5$, above the top of the wave. No solutions, so statement 3 holds.

**Notice** that statement 1 and statement 2 look contradictory, but they are about **different** values of $c$. Two "for some" statements
do not have to share their witness.
:::

## Question 18 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q16</span>

::: {.question}
$p$ and $q$ are real numbers, and the equation

$$x\lvert x\rvert=px+q$$

has exactly $k$ distinct real solutions for $x$.

Which one of the following is the complete list of **possible** values for $k$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $0,1,2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $0,1,2,3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $0,1,2,3,4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $0,2,4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $1,2,3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $1,2,3,4$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E — $1,2,3$.**

**"Possible" splits into two jobs.** A value of $k$ is possible when **there exist** $p,q$ giving it, so including a value needs one
example. Excluding a value needs an argument **for all** $p,q$.

**Step 1 — the curve.** $y=x\lvert x\rvert$ is $y=x^2$ for $x\ge0$ and $y=-x^2$ for $x<0$. It rises through the origin.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-3.2,3.2,800); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0,4.2))
ax.plot(x,x*np.abs(x),color='#1f77b4',lw=2.4,label='$y=x|x|$')
ax.plot(x,0*x+1,color='#2ca02c',lw=1.6,label='$y=1$: $k=1$')
ax.plot(x,2*x-1,color='#d62728',lw=1.6,label='$y=2x-1$: tangent, $k=2$')
ax.plot(x,x,color='#7a5195',lw=1.6,label='$y=x$: $k=3$')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.8',lw=.8); ax.axvline(0,color='0.8',lw=.8); ax.set_ylim(-7,7); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9,loc='upper left')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Step 2 — $k=0$ is impossible.** $x\lvert x\rvert-px-q$ is continuous, and the $x^2$ term dominates for large $\lvert x\rvert$: it tends to $+\infty$ as $x\to\infty$
and to $-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$. So it is zero somewhere, for all $p,q$.

**Step 3 — $k\ge4$ is impossible.** The solutions come from two quadratics:

$$x\ge0:\ \ x^2-px-q=0,\qquad\qquad x<0:\ \ x^2+px+q=0 .$$

- If $q>0$, the first quadratic has product of roots $-q<0$, so it has exactly **one** positive root. The second gives at most two. Total at most $3$.
- If $q<0$, the second quadratic has product of roots $q<0$, so it has exactly **one** negative root. The first gives at most two. Total at most $3$.
- If $q=0$, the equation is $x\lvert x\rvert=px$. Then $x=0$ is a solution, and for $x\ne0$ we need $\lvert x\rvert=p$, which has at most two solutions. Total at most $3$.

**Step 4 — $k=1,2,3$ all occur.**

| $k$ | Example | Solutions |
|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $p=0,\ q=1$ | $x=1$ only |
| $2$ | $p=2,\ q=-1$ | $x=1$ (a tangent point) and $x=-1-\sqrt2$ |
| $3$ | $p=1,\ q=0$ | $x=-1,\ 0,\ 1$ |

So the complete list is $1,2,3$.

*Check of $k=2$:* for $x\ge0$, $x^2-2x+1=(x-1)^2=0$ gives $x=1$. For $x<0$, $x^2+2x-1=0$ gives $x=-1\pm\sqrt2$, and only $-1-\sqrt2$ is negative.
:::

## Question 19 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock E · P2 Q16</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f$ be a positive function defined on $[0,\infty)$ and twice differentiable on $(0,\infty)$. Define

$$I=\int_0^4f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,$$

and let $J_n$ be the trapezium rule estimate of $I$ using $n$ strips of equal width, where $n$ is a positive integer.

Which of the following statements are **necessarily** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** If $f''(x)>0$ **for all** $0<x<4$, then $J_n>I$ **for every** positive integer $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** If $f''(x)\ge0$ and $f'(x)>0$ **for all** $0<x<4$, then $J_{n+1}<J_n$ **for every** positive integer $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** If $I<J_n$ **for some** positive integer $n$, then $\displaystyle\int_0^4f(4-x)\,\mathrm{d}x<J_{n+1}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (1) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** (2) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** (3) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** (1) and (2) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** (1) and (3) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** (2) and (3) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** none of them.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** all of them
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A — (1) only.**

**(1) is true.** $f''>0$ means that the graph curves upward, so on each strip the chord joining the endpoints lies above the
curve. So each trapezium has more area than the curve beneath it, and adding up the strips gives $J_n>I$. The argument
never used the value of $n$, so it covers **every** $n$.

**(2) is false.** It is a "for all $f$" and "for every $n$" statement, so one function at one $n$ breaks it. Take $f(x)=x+1$.
It is positive, with $f''=0\ge0$ and $f'=1>0$. The trapezium rule is exact for a straight line, so

$$J_{n+1}=J_n=I ,$$

and $J_{n+1}<J_n$ fails. The "$\ge0$" in the hypothesis is exactly what lets this example in.

**(3) is false.** First simplify. Substituting $u=4-x$ reflects the curve without changing the area, so

$$\int_0^4f(4-x)\,\mathrm{d}x=I .$$

Statement (3) is therefore: if $I<J_n$ for some $n$, then $I<J_{n+1}$ for that same $n$. In words, an overestimate
stays an overestimate with one more strip. With no condition on the curvature of $f$, it need not. Take

$$f(x)=2+2x-\frac{\big(x(4-x)\big)^3}{64} .$$

This is positive on $[0,\infty)$: on $[0,4]$ the fraction is at most $1$, so $f\ge1$, and for $x>4$ the fraction is negative. It has $f(0)=2,\ f(2)=5,\ f(4)=10$.

$$J_1=\frac{4}{2}(2+10)=24,\qquad J_2=\frac{2}{2}\big(2+2\times5+10\big)=22,\qquad I=\frac{776}{35}\approx22.17 .$$

So $J_1>I$ but $J_2<I$, and (3) fails at $n=1$: the extra midpoint falls in the dip and drags the estimate from above $I$ to below it.

**The quantifier point.** In (1) and (2), "for every $n$" is in the **conclusion**, so you must cover all $n$. In (3), "for some $n$" is in
the **hypothesis**, so you are simply handed one $n$. Only then is $J_{n+1}$ compared, using that same $n$.
:::
